questions.question: State the assumptions of perfect competition and explain, with reference to the industry and the individual business, why the firm's demand curve is horizontal and what that line represents.
questions.expected_answer: Assumptions: very many buyers and sellers each too small to influence price; a homogeneous product; free entry and exit; perfect knowledge of prices; mobile factors of production, with no collusion or government interference. The industry's downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply curves set the equilibrium market price. The individual business must accept that price: with identical products and perfectly informed buyers, charging even slightly more sells nothing, while charging less sacrifices revenue on units it could already sell at the market price. It is a price taker whose only decision is quantity. Its demand curve is therefore a horizontal line at the market price, and that one line is simultaneously the demand curve, the average revenue curve (each unit sells at the same price) and the marginal revenue curve (each extra unit adds exactly the price): D = AR = MR = P.

questions.question: Explain how the perfectly competitive firm determines its output, and distinguish normal profit, economic profit and economic loss, including the shut-down decision.
questions.expected_answer: The firm produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost with MC rising — in perfect competition, where the rising MC curve cuts the horizontal price line. Any unit whose extra revenue exceeds its extra cost adds to profit; the first unit costing more than it earns subtracts, so output stops at the crossing. Normal profit is the minimum earning needed to keep the entrepreneur in the industry — the opportunity cost of capital and enterprise — and is included in the cost curves; it is earned when price equals average cost at the chosen output. Economic (supernormal) profit exists when price exceeds average cost — on the diagram a rectangle between the price line and AC, per-unit surplus times output. An economic loss occurs when price is below average cost. A loss-making firm should still produce in the short run if price covers average variable cost, because fixed costs are owed anyway and each unit then contributes toward them; if price falls below minimum AVC every unit deepens the loss and the firm shuts down. Hence the firm's supply curve is its MC curve above minimum AVC.

questions.question: Describe long-run equilibrium in a perfect market and explain how South Africa's competition policy institutions attempt to push real markets toward that benchmark.
questions.expected_answer: With free entry and perfect knowledge, economic profit attracts newcomers, shifting industry supply right and lowering price; losses cause exit, shifting supply left and raising price. The process rests where price just touches minimum average cost: every firm earns normal profit only, price equals marginal cost (allocative efficiency — resources follow consumers' wishes) and output occurs at minimum average cost (productive efficiency). Real markets fall short, so the Competition Act of 1998 created three institutions: the Competition Commission investigates mergers, cartels and markets; the Competition Tribunal adjudicates and can block mergers, impose conditions and fine firms up to ten percent of annual turnover; the Competition Appeal Court hears appeals. The Act attacks horizontal collusion (price fixing, market division, bid rigging — as in the bread cartel and World Cup construction cases), vertical restrictive practices, abuse of dominance, and anti-competitive mergers, with South African merger law also weighing public interest such as employment and small-business access. The rationale in model terms: collusion turns many price takers into one price maker, restricting output and raising price above marginal cost; policy restores by law the discipline that many rivals and free entry provide automatically in the model.
